newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SNB has no plans to change rates near-term - Roth.
newsitem.headline: SNB has no plans to change rates near-term - Roth.

text.p: Swiss National Bank (SNB) vice chairman Jean-Pierre Roth said the central bank had no plans to change its interest rates near-term.

Roth, speaking to reporters before a talk here said: "There is no reason to expect interest rates to move in one direction or the other. If there is pressure on the Swiss franc due to uncertainty surrounding monetary union, we would be ready to reconsider monetary policy."
"But we don't see that now," Roth added.
"We have no intention to change monetary policy," Roth said.
Asked if there was need for an interest rate increase, he said: "At the moment, we have no reason to do that."
He said that "things are more or less stable at the moment. There is no pressure on the markets in one direction or the other. There is no reason for reacting at the moment."

The SNB has said in the past that it would consider easing if the Swiss franc were to see strong upward pressure tied to turbulence amidst planned start of the single European currency, the euro. A stronger franc tends to hurt Swiss exports and would weigh on the country's budding recovery.
It has also said it would have to tighten at some point when the Swiss recovery becomes more advanced. But SNB chairman Hans Meyer said last week that it was too early in the cycle to tighten.
The Swiss discount rate, last changed when it was cut by half a percentage point on September 26 to 1.00 percent, now matches historic lows.
With respect to Swiss growth, Roth reiterated the SNB's forecast for 0.5 percent gross domestic product growth in 1997.
He said the prospects for recovery in Europe outside of Switzerland were also "nothing spectacular," a factor weighing on domestic growth.

"For us, there is no nice weather in Switzerland if the weather is bad or not that nice abroad. We are going to try to have an acceleration of growth for the entire year, so we can overall, in 1997, be above zero," Roth said.
